passage:
Dear Vishal,

I've started this letter four times. I'm writing because I ended things on Friday and then said almost nothing, and that wasn't fair to you. You deserved a clear reason, and here it is: I'm not in the same place you are, and I don't want to keep going just because it feels easier than hurting you. I can't stop thinking about how your face changed when I said it. I feel awful. I also know saying sorry many times isn't going to make it better, so I won't keep texting you. I won't send mixed messages or ask to stay friends before you're ready. I still think you're kind and funny, and I'm sorry it took me so long to be honest. I'll give you all the space you need.

Rajni

qa.q: What did Rajni do on Friday, according to the letter?
qa.a: Rajni ended the relationship with Vishal.

qa.q: What is Rajni feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Guilty and sad. Rajni writes about feeling awful and not being able to stop thinking about how Vishal's face changed.

qa.q: What makes this letter a respectful way to end things?
qa.a: It is honest and clear, gives a reason without blame, promises no mixed messages and offers space instead of pushing for friendship or ghosting.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel reading it?
qa.a: Probably hurt, but Vishal may also feel respected, because the letter gives a clear reason and does not leave Vishal guessing.

grounding: Rajni ended the relationship, feels guilty for the pain, and writes honestly and respectfully with no mixed messages and space for the other person.

passage:
Okay, Kevin, you asked, so here's the honest version. I'm Joseph, and three months ago I broke up with Lavanya.
We'd been together almost a year. Somewhere around Diwali I realised I didn't feel the same anymore. And I felt terrible even thinking it, because she's lovely. She did nothing wrong.
The easy thing would have been to just go quiet. Reply late, reply less, let her figure it out. A lot of people do that. I almost did.
But I asked her to meet at the park near her house. I said it straight: "I don't feel the same way anymore. It's not anything you did. I'm really sorry." She cried. I felt awful watching her.
Then the hardest part: I didn't text her that night asking if she was okay, even though I wanted to. That would've been mixed messages. I gave her space. Now we nod at each other in class, and that's fine.

qa.q: Where did Joseph and Lavanya meet to talk?
qa.a: At the park near her house.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel about ending things?
qa.a: Joseph felt guilty and awful, because Lavanya had done nothing wrong and cried when Joseph told her.

qa.q: Which choices made Joseph's breakup respectful?
qa.a: Joseph told Lavanya face to face and honestly, didn't blame her, didn't ghost, and gave her space instead of sending mixed messages.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lavanya if Joseph had simply gone quiet?
qa.a: She would have been confused and hurt, left guessing what was wrong, which would have been crueller than an honest talk.

grounding: A teen who ends a relationship feels guilty but is honest and respectful, avoids mixed messages and gives space instead of ghosting.

passage:
Monday. Suraj realised he didn't want to be with Sangeeta anymore. He felt awful. She'd made him a birthday card only last week. For two days he replied to her with just "ok" and "hmm," hoping she'd understand without him saying anything.
Wednesday. Sangeeta messaged: "Did I do something?" Suraj stared at it and felt sick. He was ghosting her, slowly. He asked her to meet at the library steps after school. He told her plainly: "I don't want to be in the relationship anymore. You didn't do anything wrong. I'm sorry I went quiet instead of telling you." She looked away and nodded, eyes wet.
Saturday. He wanted badly to message her, "Are you okay?" He didn't. He knew it would only confuse things. When he saw her at the tuition centre, he just smiled politely and sat on the other side, giving her space.

qa.q: Where did Suraj and Sangeeta meet to talk?
qa.a: At the library steps after school.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when Sangeeta asked 'Did I do something?'
qa.a: He felt sick and guilty, realising his short replies were a slow way of ghosting her.

qa.q: What did Suraj change, and why was it better?
qa.a: He stopped the vague replies and told Sangeeta honestly in person, then gave her space, which was clearer and more respectful than ghosting.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt during the days of short replies?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably felt confused and anxious, wondering if she had done something wrong.

grounding: A teen who ends a relationship feels guilty, stops ghosting, tells her honestly and gives her space.
